newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Copper falls, wheat jumps in commodities.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Copper falls, wheat jumps in commodities.

text.p: World copper prices dropped sharply on Wednesday on signs of a buildup in stocks and production of the metal just as demand makes its seasonal decline in the U.S. and European summer.
Elsewhere in commodity markets, Chicago wheat prices rose on talk of potential Middle East imports. Gold did not for the moment extend its dramatic fall of recent days.
Copper on the London Metal Exchange (LME) was sold down to $2,230 per tonne, a 4-1/2 months low.
"If the market is going to turn, then this is the time of the year when it should be turning," Angus MacMillan of LME trader Billiton Metals said.
"The bulls have been fighting a rearguard battle," said MacMillan.
Although U.S. demand is slowing, copper bulls were pinning their hopes on China taking up the slack, but the Chinese are now selling metal, he noted.
And recent data issued by the International Copper Study Group (ICSG) shows that the market was more or less balanced during the first part of the year, MacMillan said.
Jan/April copper consumption was 4.406 million tonnes, against total refined production of 4.377 million tonnes, the ICSG figures show.
Gold prices edged just higher from a day's low on Wednesday afternoon but the market was still hanging on by a thread above recent 12-year lows, dealers said.
Gold was fixed in London at $317.30 an ounce after $315.75 in the morning and later edged up to $319.

Prices nosedived last week after the Australian central bank announced it had sold 167 tonnes of gold from its reserves. The move was seen as the final straw for an already bearish market anxious about the prospect of central banks unloading gold stocks.
Chicago Board of Trade wheat futures rallied strongly in fast trading on fund buying, with talk that Egypt was seeking U.S. wheat also cited, traders said.
This could not be confirmed.
The market was technically oversold and due for a rally, and some traders expected that rainfall in the U.S. Midwest would slow wheat harvesting.
July CBOT soft red winter wheat futures were soon up by almost 10 cents to $3.34 per bushel.
Some key prices at 1645 GMT.
